title: Tears and Tears
intro: Badawi al-Jabal published this poem as “Tears and Tears” in the magazine al-Irfan in December 1923; in it he says he is nineteen, and the same issue describes him as a youth of nineteen. His diwan (Dar al-Awda, Beirut, 1978) prints it among his early verse, in the section called al-Bawakir, “First Fruits”, dated 1925 and in a text that differs from the magazine's in places; the reciter follows the diwan. It is built in stanzas, each with its own rhyme, and after every stanza the opening line to the nightingale returns with a second line as a refrain, and al-Irfan's index calls it a muwashshah; Nabil Sulayman notes that such changing stanzas, refrains and rhymes are frequent in the poet's early work, finds their nearest precedent in the muwashshah, and observes that they fade from his later poetry. The poet first sets the carefree bird against his own grief and the disasters that have settled on his land, then mourns the lost glory of the Arabs, from Harun al-Rashid's crown to the palace-city of al-Zahra', the Umayyads and the Hamdanids, weeps over the conquerors' graves at Yarmuk and Qadisiyya, and ends with his beloved Layla in tears as he resolves to go to war, asking her to keep faith if he dies far from home. Rabih Farruji reads the refrain as a struggle between the call to sing, which for him is a call to resist, and the words of grief and surrender around it, a struggle the call to sing wins.

translation: Sing, nightingale, high in the great trees, sing:
love and poetry are more yours than mine.
1.sharh: He calls on the nightingale to sing and grants that love and poetry belong to it more than to him, since its song carries no grief. This line opens the poem and comes back after every stanza as the first half of its refrain.

translation: You have a magic like mine, a wonder;
do you find in you a sorrow like mine?
2.sharh: The bird's song and the poet's verse cast the same spell. What he doubts is that the bird shares his grief, and that difference between them runs through the whole poem.

translation: So trill your songs of love,
at ease as long as you like, from branch to branch.
3.sharh: He lets the bird sing of love as long as it pleases, moving at ease from branch to branch. The command is a concession: the bird may keep the carefree song the poet cannot have.

translation: And learn how a poet weeps
who is lost between coldness and unjust blame.
4.sharh: In return the bird can learn from him how a poet weeps, a poet worn down by a beloved who turns away from him and finds fault where there is none. Grief is the one thing he can teach the bird.

translation: The world (and in the like of it lie
the world's lessons and the echoes of wishing)
5.sharh: This line begins a sentence that ends in the next: the world is a raid. Between subject and predicate he sets an aside: in the like of this world lie the lessons it teaches and the echoes of hope. The line gives “the world” no predicate of its own, so the likelier reading takes “a raid”, which opens the next line, as its end; no commentary on the poem exists to settle it.

translation: is a raid whose embers I did not fear,
but my sword glanced off and my shield did not hold.
6.sharh: Life, for him, has been a raid he rode into without fear of its fire, and lost: his sword failed to bite and his shield gave way. The images of battle prepare the turn to his country's troubles in the lines that follow.

translation: Many a dire calamity has settled on the homeland
(its guardian gone), and many a crushing disaster.
7.sharh: Disasters have come to rest on his land like camels made to kneel, while the one who should defend it is absent. The diwan sets “its guardian gone” between dashes, an aside that makes the calamity worse.

translation: Between what I hear and what I see, I wish
my eye did not see, nor my ear hear.
8.sharh: Some of these disasters reach him as news and some he sees for himself, and he wishes he were blind and deaf to them all. The wish is the measure of his anguish.

translation: What blame is there on my song, now I have sent it out?
My song sets the world on fire against the usurper.
9.sharh: Once released, his song is beyond reproach, for it rouses everyone against the one who has taken the homeland. The first half may also ask what his song is bound to do, with the second as the answer. Unlike the nightingale's, his singing is a weapon.

translation: If I do not stir it to resolve,
may my flint strike no fire and my pillar cast no shade.
10.sharh: He stakes his worth on this: if his poetry fails to rouse the world, may he never succeed at anything. A flint that sparks stands for success, and a pillar that gives shade for a man others can shelter behind.

translation: You know nothing of the world's cares, so take,
O bird, your lessons in grief from me.
11.sharh: The bird knows nothing of the world's troubles, and the poet offers to teach it. With the opening line this makes up the refrain heard after each stanza, and it returns to the offer of line 4: the poet has much to teach the bird about sorrow.

translation: Harun's crown has lost its gleam,
and the Tigris wept for grief, and the Euphrates.
12.sharh: Harun al-Rashid's crown has gone dark, and the two rivers of Iraq weep for it. With this line the second stanza turns to the lost glory of the Arabs, beginning with the Abbasid caliphate at its height.

translation: The heights of al-Zahra' have fallen, though once
they vied in height with the bright, shining stars.
13.sharh: From the Abbasid east he turns to the Umayyads of al-Andalus and their palace-city of al-Zahra', whose towers once rose to the stars and have now fallen. The line plays on the name al-Zahra', “the shining”, and the “shining” (zuhr) stars.

translation: The sons of Marwan have turned away and are gone,
and have left the backs of their noble steeds.
14.sharh: The Umayyads too have passed away and have dismounted from the horses that carried their conquests. Giving up the saddle stands for giving up the power it won.

translation: Tell the Byzantine army: what is there to fear?
The turns of fate have treacherously swept the raiders away.
15.sharh: He taunts the Byzantines, old enemies of the caliphs and of the Hamdanids: they have nothing left to fear, for fate has treacherously destroyed the Arab raiders who once marched against them.

translation: Neither the sons of Abbas in the crush of battle,
no, nor the proud sons of Hamdan.
16.sharh: This answers the taunt: none of those the Byzantines feared remain, neither the caliphs of Baghdad nor the princes of Aleppo who fought them.

translation: Hobbled between the tents at the valley's bend
and the two rivers stand the finest racers.
17.sharh: The thoroughbreds that once carried the raids now stand hobbled in the camps, from the desert to the rivers of Iraq: the Arabs no longer ride out to war. The idle horses go with the rusted swords of the next line.

translation: And the swords in their scabbards
have rusted: woe is me for those keen blades.
18.sharh: Left unused, the swords have rusted in their sheaths, and he cries out in grief for blades once sharp enough to cut anything. Hobbled horses and rusted swords close the stanza on an Arab world that no longer fights.

translation: Stand at Yarmuk, humbled and weeping,
and take your ablution from the soil of Qadisiyya.
19.sharh: He bids the listener stand at Yarmuk in awe and tears, and purify himself with the soil of Qadisiyya as one does with clean earth before prayer when there is no water. The two fields where the early Muslims defeated Byzantium and Persia become holy ground.

translation: Soil good and pure,
and graves drenched by a rain of tears.
20.sharh: The earth of these battlefields is pure enough for the ablution, and the graves in it are watered by tears as if by rain. “Good soil” echoes the Quran's “good earth” in the verse on dry ablution, completing the image of the line before.

translation: Here lie the brave chiefs
who forcibly wrenched back the reins of the Age of Ignorance.
21.sharh: These are the graves of the heroes who forced the pagan age to turn back, mastering it like a runaway horse pulled round by its reins.

translation: They subdued the Byzantines and toppled their throne,
and furled the red banners of Persia.
22.sharh: The two battles of the stanza are matched: Yarmuk broke the Byzantines, and Qadisiyya furled the Persian standards. To topple someone's throne, in Arabic idiom, is to bring his kingdom down.

translation: O graves effaced and worn away,
you are the lamp of faith and of love of country.
23.sharh: The conquerors' graves have vanished from sight, yet he calls them a lamp that still guides, in faith and in patriotism. He sets love of country beside religion as the two lights they give.

translation: When the rain holds back, you shall have from my tears
a steady shower that weeps, and a low, brimming cloud.
24.sharh: If the rain fails the graves, his tears will water them instead, as steadily and as heavily as the best of rains. He offers his weeping in place of the rain that keeps graves green.

translation: They have seen my Layla shedding her tears;
may God honour those pure tears.
25.sharh: The last stanza turns to love: people have seen his beloved weeping, and he blesses her tears. The title, “Tears and Tears”, may set his tears for the graves beside hers for him.

translation: May God guard the eyelids that have scented
those fresh cheeks with dew.
26.sharh: He prays for the eyes that wet her cheeks. The tears are dew, and her cheeks the flowers whose scent the dew brings out.

translation: Hold back your tears, so that no eye sees them,
not even the shining stars.
27.sharh: He asks her to dry her eyes so that no one, not even the stars, sees her weep. Her tears are his to guard, like her.

translation: Daughter of my love, I have a resolve
that breaks calamity, and a rebellious soul.
28.sharh: He comforts her with his own strength: a will that snaps misfortune like a thorny branch, and a spirit in revolt. She has no cause to weep for a man made like this.

translation: I see myself tomorrow charging in,
shaded by cutting swords.
29.sharh: He pictures himself going into battle, with so many blades raised over him that they shade him like a canopy. The picture of his courage is meant to answer Layla's tears.

translation: throwing myself into the thick of it,
whichever way the wheel turns there.
30.sharh: He will throw himself where the battle is fiercest, whatever the outcome. “It” is the battle implied by the charge in the line before, or else the swords just named; either way he means where the blows fall thickest.

translation: And if I die a stranger, far from home,
nineteen years of age,
31.sharh: He imagines dying in battle far from home, and gives his age, nineteen; the request this leads to follows in the next two lines.

translation: remember me, keep faith with our love,
and mourn the bad luck of stumbling fortunes.
32.sharh: He asks that she remember him, stay true to their love, and lament the ill luck that would cut him down so young. He lays the death he foresees at the door of fortune.

translation: By God, I am no faithless lover;
do not be faithless after I am dead.
33.sharh: He swears he has kept faith with her, and asks her to do the same once he is gone. The refrain then returns to close the poem.

1.1.3.meaning: Bulbul: a songbird with a fine voice; the nightingale.

1.1.5.meaning: Great spreading trees; the singular is dawha.

2.1.2.meaning: Magic: here the enchantment of song and speech.

2.1.3.meaning: Like: the reciter says mithla; the diwan prints mithlu. The meaning is the same.

4.2.5.head: تَجَنّي
4.2.5.meaning: Unjust blame: charging someone with a fault they did not commit.

5.2.3.head: صَدى
5.2.3.meaning: Echoes: the sound that comes back from a mountainside; here what remains of wishes once they have failed.

6.1.1.meaning: A raid: a sudden attack on horseback.

6.2.1-2.head: نَبا سَيفي
6.2.1-2.meaning: “My sword glanced off”: it bounced off without cutting.

7.1.3.head: أَناخَ
7.1.3.meaning: Settled: anakha is to make a camel kneel.

7.1.4.head: الحِمى
7.1.4.meaning: The protected ground; here the homeland.

7.2.4.meaning: Crushing: so heavy that it sways under its own weight.

9.2.4.meaning: The usurper: one who seizes what is not his by force.

10.2.1-3.meaning: “May my flint strike no fire”: a curse on himself, may nothing he tries succeed.

12.1.2.meaning: Harun al-Rashid (149–193 AH, 766–809 CE), the fifth Abbasid caliph and, al-Zirikli says, the most famous.

13.1.2.meaning: Al-Zahra': a small city near Cordoba in al-Andalus, laid out by the Umayyad Abd al-Rahman al-Nasir in 325 AH (936–937 CE).

14.1.2.meaning: Banu Marwan: the Umayyad caliphs descended from Marwan ibn al-Hakam (d. 65 AH, 685 CE), and through him the rulers of al-Andalus. The poem's first printing, in al-Irfan (1923), has Banu Ayyub, the Ayyubids, here.

14.2.4.head: الصّافِن
14.2.4.meaning: Steeds: literally horses standing on three legs with the fourth hoof tipped; the Quran uses the word of fine horses (38:31).

15.1.3.meaning: Rum: the Byzantines. The caliph al-Mahdi sent his son Harun against them, and Sayf al-Dawla fought them many times.

15.2.2-3.head: رَيب الدَّهر
15.2.2-3.meaning: “The turns of fate”: the blows of time.

16.1.3.meaning: The sons of Abbas: the Abbasid caliphs, Harun al-Rashid among them.

16.1.6.meaning: Battle; first the din of battle.

16.2.4.meaning: The sons of Hamdan: the Hamdanid princes, among them Sayf al-Dawla (303–356 AH, 915–967 CE), prince of Aleppo.

17.1.1.head: عَقِلَ
17.1.1.meaning: Hobbled: the reciter says aqilat, “went crook-legged”, said of a camel whose legs are twisted; the diwan's passive uqilat, “were hobbled”, tied with a foreleg folded so they cannot run, is likelier what the poet meant.

17.1.4.meaning: The valley's bend: here the desert camps.

17.2.1.head: الفُراتان
17.2.1.meaning: The two rivers: the Euphrates and the Dujayl, or by some accounts the Euphrates and the Tigris; here Iraq.

18.2.3.head: وَيلَة
18.2.3.meaning: “Woe is me”: a cry of grief; the Quran has it as ya waylata (11:72, 25:28).

19.1.3.meaning: Yarmuk: a valley in Syria at the edge of the Ghawr, running into the Jordan, where the Muslims fought the Byzantines.

19.2.1.head: تَيَمَّم
19.2.1.meaning: Take your ablution: wipe face and hands with clean earth, the dry ablution allowed when there is no water (Quran 4:43, 5:6).

19.2.4.meaning: Qadisiyya: a place fifteen farsakhs from Kufa where Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and the Muslims defeated the Persians under the caliph Umar, in 16 AH (637 CE) by Yaqut's dating.

20.1.2.meaning: Good: the diwan prints tiba, which breaks the meter; the reciter says tayyiba.

21.2.4.meaning: The reins; to twist someone's reins (lawa inanahu) is to turn him from his course.

21.2.5.meaning: The Jahiliyya, “the Age of Ignorance”: Arabia before Islam.

22.1.1.head: دَوَّخَ
22.1.1.meaning: Subdued: crushed and brought under their rule.

22.2.3.head: البَند
22.2.3.meaning: Banners: the word is itself borrowed from Persian.

24.2.3.head: وَطفاء
24.2.3.meaning: A cloud hanging low with the weight of its water.

27.1.1.meaning: Hold back: wipe away and stop.

28.2.1.head: خَضَدَ
28.2.1.meaning: Breaks: the verb is used of breaking a branch or stripping its thorns.

30.1.4.head: غَمرَة
30.1.4.meaning: The thick of it: the worst of the fighting.

30.2.4.meaning: The wheel: defeat, or the turn of fortune.

31.2.3-5.meaning: “In the ninth after the tenth”: nineteen.

32.2.1.head: اُندُبي
32.2.1.meaning: Mourn: lament, as one laments the dead by recounting their virtues.

32.2.3.head: الجَدّ
32.2.3.meaning: Fortunes: judud, plural of jadd, luck, not of jadd, grandfather.
